steps.title: Learning, not medical advice

steps.title: Two kinds of numbers
steps.body: **Perfect use** = failure rate when a method is used exactly right every time. **Typical use** = what happens in real life, including forgotten pills and condoms put on late. Typical use is the number that matters for planning.

steps.title: Approximate typical-use pregnancies per 100 users in a year (WHO/CDC-type figures)
steps.body:
- Implant: under 1
- Hormonal or copper IUD: under 1
- Sterilisation (vasectomy or tubal): under 1
- Injectable (e.g. DMPA, 'Antara' in the government programme): about 4
- Pill, patch, ring: about 7
- Male condom: about 13
- Withdrawal: about 20
- Female condom: about 21
- Fertility-awareness methods: roughly 2–23 depending on method and discipline

steps.title: The 'forgettable' principle
steps.body: Methods you do not have to remember (implant, IUD, sterilisation) are the most effective in real life because human error is removed.

steps.title: Only condoms protect against STIs
steps.body: No hormonal method, IUD or sterilisation protects against STIs or HIV. Many couples use condoms *plus* another method ('dual protection').

statements.s: A condom's typical-use failure is higher than its perfect-use failure.
statements.why: Late application, breakage and slipping all happen in real life.

statements.s: The pill protects against STIs.
statements.why: Only barrier methods (condoms) reduce STI risk.

statements.s: An IUD is among the most effective reversible methods.
statements.why: Under 1 pregnancy per 100 users per year.

statements.s: Withdrawal is as effective as the pill.
statements.why: Typical-use failure is about 20 per 100 versus about 7.

quiz.why: Typical use includes ordinary human mistakes.

steps.title: Hormonal methods
steps.body: **Combined methods** (pill, patch, ring) contain oestrogen + progestogen and mainly stop ovulation. **Progestogen-only** methods (mini-pill, injectable, implant, hormonal IUD) thicken cervical mucus and may stop ovulation. India's public programme also offers **centchroman ('Chhaya')**, a non-steroidal weekly pill.

steps.title: Non-hormonal methods
steps.body: **Copper IUD**: copper is toxic to sperm; works for 5–10 years depending on type. **Condoms** (male/female): barrier. **Sterilisation**: vasectomy (blocks the vas deferens; a semen test is needed before relying on it) or tubal ligation — intended as permanent.

steps.title: Combined oestrogen methods are not for everyone
steps.body: Doctors avoid combined methods for people with migraine with aura, a past blood clot, some heart conditions, smokers over 35, and in the first weeks after childbirth. Progestogen-only or copper methods are often options instead.

steps.title: Common, usually harmless side effects
steps.body: Irregular spotting (implant, injectable, mini-pill), heavier periods (copper IUD), breast tenderness or nausea early on (combined pill). Many settle in 3 months. Fertility returns quickly after most methods; after the injectable it can take several months.

steps.title: Switching
steps.body: Switch with your doctor's guidance so there is no gap in protection — many switches are 'start the new method before stopping the old'.

steps.title: Myth: the pill makes you infertile
steps.body: False. Fertility returns soon after stopping the pill — often within the next cycle.

steps.title: Myth: an IUD causes abortion or infertility
steps.body: False. IUDs prevent fertilisation; they are not abortion. Fertility returns after removal. A small infection risk exists around insertion, which is why STI screening is offered when needed.

steps.title: Myth: you can't get pregnant during your period or the first time
steps.body: False. Sperm can survive up to about 5 days, and cycles vary. The first time carries the same risk as any other time.

steps.title: The pill and cancer
steps.body: Combined pill use is linked with *lower* lifetime risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer and a small, temporary rise in breast-cancer risk while using it. Discuss your personal history with a doctor.

steps.title: Check sources
steps.body: Prefer your doctor, a government health centre, or WHO/ICMR material over forwards and social media.

steps.title: Options
steps.body:
- **Levonorgestrel EC pill**: a single-dose tablet sold at pharmacies; licensed for use up to 72 hours (3 days); works best the sooner it is taken.
- **Copper IUD** inserted by a clinician within 5 days: the most effective emergency method, and it then continues as contraception.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: EC pills mainly delay or prevent ovulation. They do **not** end an established pregnancy and are not abortion pills.

steps.title: Not for regular use
steps.body: EC is a backup, not a routine method — it is less effective than regular contraception. Repeated use is not dangerous but is unreliable.

steps.title: After EC
steps.body: The next period may be a few days early or late. Take a pregnancy test if the period is more than 7 days late, or very light. Consider an STI test if the risk applies.

EC pills cause abortion.

lessons.title: STIs: the silent ones and the noticeable ones

scenes.text: Vikram, 29, feels fine but his new partner asks him to get tested.
'I'd know if I had something,' he says.
His test shows chlamydia — with zero symptoms.

steps.title: Often no symptoms
steps.body: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea (especially in women), HPV, early HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis can be silent. That is why testing, not feeling, tells you your status.

steps.title: Possible symptoms
steps.body: Unusual discharge, burning when passing urine, sores or blisters, warts, pelvic pain, pain during sex, rashes, swollen glands. Any of these deserves a clinic visit.

steps.title: Treatable vs manageable
steps.body: **Curable** with the right antibiotics: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, trichomoniasis. **Manageable** with medicines: herpes, HIV (modern treatment lets people live long, healthy lives; with an undetectable viral load HIV is not transmitted sexually — 'U=U'), hepatitis B. Partners also need treatment to avoid re-infection.

steps.title: Untreated infections
steps.body: Untreated chlamydia/gonorrhoea can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility. Syphilis in pregnancy can harm the baby — which is why antenatal screening is routine.

lessons.title: Testing, PEP, PrEP and the HPV vaccine

scenes.text: Farah, 24, is nervous about going to an STI clinic.
She finds a government ICTC (Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre) where HIV testing is free and confidential.
The counsellor is kind; it takes under an hour.

steps.title: Where to test
steps.body: Government ICTCs and 'Suraksha' STI clinics offer free, confidential testing; private labs and gynaecologists/dermato-venereologists also test. National AIDS helpline: **1097**.

steps.title: Window periods
steps.body: Tests need time after exposure to detect infection. Modern HIV combination tests detect most infections by about 6 weeks; a negative test soon after a risk is often repeated later, as advised by the clinic.

steps.title: PEP and PrEP
steps.body: **PEP** (post-exposure prophylaxis) is a 28-day course of HIV medicines started as soon as possible and within **72 hours** after a possible exposure — go to a hospital or ART centre urgently. **PrEP** is taken before possible exposure by people at ongoing higher risk, under medical supervision.

steps.title: HPV vaccine
steps.body: HPV causes almost all cervical cancer and some throat, anal and penile cancers. Vaccination works best before any sexual activity (WHO prioritises girls aged 9–14) but adults can discuss catch-up vaccination with a doctor. India has an indigenous HPV vaccine. Vaccinated women still need cervical screening.

activity.prompt: Questions people are too shy to ask at an STI clinic

items.q: Will they tell my family?
items.a: No. Testing is confidential; results are given to you.

items.q: Do I have to describe what I did?
items.a: Only what's needed to choose the right tests — staff hear this every day and won't judge.

items.q: I'm married. Can I still get an STI?
items.a: Yes. Marital status doesn't protect anyone; testing before or within a relationship is responsible.

items.q: Is a pap/HPV test painful?
items.a: Usually brief discomfort, not pain. Tell the clinician if you are anxious — they can go slowly.

quiz.why: Sooner is better; 72 hours is the outer limit.

lessons.title: Consent is ongoing — even after 10 years

scenes.text: Anil assumes 'we're married, so yes is always yes'.
Poonam often feels too tired but says nothing.
A counsellor helps them talk about it openly.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What consent means
steps.body: Consent is **freely given, informed, enthusiastic, specific and reversible**. It is given each time, can be withdrawn at any moment, and saying yes to one thing is not yes to everything.

steps.title: Silence is not consent
steps.body: Being tired, asleep, drunk or quietly going along to avoid a fight is not freely given consent. Check in: 'Are you up for this?' 'Want to stop?'

steps.title: Coercion
steps.body: Pressure, guilt-tripping, threats, sulking until someone gives in, or making them 'owe' you are forms of coercion — they harm trust and wellbeing.

steps.title: Law in general terms
steps.body: Indian law criminalises sexual assault and provides protection from domestic violence (Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005). The legal position on marital rape is under judicial consideration — but ethically and for health, consent matters in every relationship. This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: Being married means consent is permanent.
statements.why: Consent is given each time and can be withdrawn.

statements.s: Someone can change their mind midway.
Sulking until a partner agrees is a form of pressure.
Checking in kills romance.
statements.why: Most couples find it builds trust and closeness.

scenes.text: Imran wants intimacy more often than Zoya.

steps.title: Mismatched desire is common
steps.body: Almost every long-term couple has periods where one partner wants sex more. It isn't a sign of a failed relationship.

steps.title: Scripts that help
steps.body:
- 'I love being close to you. Can we talk about what we each enjoy?'
- 'Not tonight — but I'd love a cuddle.' (a no to sex, a yes to closeness)
- 'What would make it easier for you to feel in the mood?'

steps.title: Rules of the talk
steps.body: Pick a calm time, not in bed right after a rejection. Use 'I' statements. Listen without arguing. Agree on one small experiment.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If talking keeps turning into fights, a couples counsellor or sex therapist can help. Sudden changes in desire can have medical causes worth checking.

steps.title: Before stopping condoms
steps.body: Both partners test for STIs including HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, agree on exclusivity honestly, and choose another contraceptive if pregnancy isn't wanted.

steps.title: Other habits
steps.body: Use water- or silicone-based lubricant with latex condoms (oil-based products like coconut oil or petroleum jelly weaken latex). Use a new condom each time. Hepatitis B vaccination is worth asking about.

steps.title: Reducing risk
steps.body: Condoms, HPV and hepatitis B vaccines, regular testing, PrEP where appropriate, and treating infections promptly together reduce STI risk a great deal.

scenes.text: Suresh, 48, has had trouble keeping an erection for months and feels ashamed.
He nearly buys a 'herbal power' remedy advertised on TV.
His GP finds high blood sugar and blood pressure instead.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Very common
steps.body: Erectile dysfunction (ED) becomes more common with age, and occasional difficulty happens to almost everyone. Persistent ED deserves a check-up.

steps.title: ED can be an early warning
steps.body: ED often comes from reduced blood flow — the same process behind heart disease. Diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, heavy drinking, some medicines, low testosterone, depression and stress are common causes.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Treating the cause, lifestyle change, counselling, and prescribed medicines (PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil or tadalafil). These must be prescribed: they are **dangerous with nitrate heart medicines**.

steps.title: Early (premature) ejaculation
steps.body: Very common, especially with anxiety or new partners. Behavioural techniques, counselling, and sometimes prescribed medicines help. It is not a disease of 'weakness'.

steps.title: Avoid quacks
steps.body: Unlabelled 'power' capsules may contain hidden prescription drugs or heavy metals. See a registered doctor, urologist or andrologist.

statements.s: ED can be an early sign of heart disease.
statements.why: Blood vessels in the penis are small and show problems early.

statements.s: ED medicines are safe with nitrate heart pills.
statements.why: The combination can drop blood pressure dangerously.

statements.s: Occasional erection problems are normal.
statements.why: Stress, tiredness and alcohol affect everyone sometimes.

statements.s: Herbal 'power' remedies sold on TV are always safe.

quiz.q: Why should persistent ED prompt a health check?
options: It can signal diabetes or heart disease

scenes.text: Anjali, 38, mother of two, says she 'just doesn't feel like it anymore'.
She worries something is wrong with her — or her marriage.
Her doctor checks thyroid, iron, medicines and mood, and asks about sleep and stress.

steps.title: Desire changes
steps.body: Desire naturally rises and falls with stress, sleep, parenting, illness, relationship conflict, hormones and age. Many people feel 'responsive desire' — interest grows after closeness starts — rather than spontaneous desire.

steps.title: Possible medical contributors
steps.body: Depression and some antidepressants, thyroid problems, anaemia, low testosterone, hormonal contraception in some people, breastfeeding, menopause, chronic pain, alcohol.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body: Treat causes, share household load, protect sleep, plan unhurried time together, communicate, and consider a sex therapist. Low desire is only a 'problem' if it bothers you.

items.q: Is it normal not to want sex for months?
items.a: It can be, especially during stress, illness or with young children. It's worth exploring if it bothers you or your partner.

items.q: Can antidepressants affect desire?
items.a: Yes, some can. Don't stop them suddenly — talk to your doctor, who may adjust the treatment.

items.q: Is asexuality a disorder?
items.a: No. Asexuality is an orientation — some people experience little or no sexual attraction and are not ill.

items.q: Does testosterone fix everything?

steps.title: Pain is a signal, not a duty

steps.title: Treatment works

steps.title: The hymen myth
steps.body: The hymen is a thin, flexible tissue that varies naturally; many women do not bleed the first time. Its appearance cannot prove whether someone has had sex.

steps.title: 'Virginity tests' are unscientific
steps.body: WHO and UN agencies have called 'virginity testing' unscientific and a human-rights violation. India's Supreme Court has condemned the 'two-finger test' and said those conducting it may be held guilty of misconduct.

steps.title: The first time
steps.body: It's normal to feel nervous. Go slowly, use lubricant, communicate, and stop if it hurts. It is not a performance; many couples take days or weeks to feel comfortable.

steps.title: Pregnancy and STIs
steps.body: Pregnancy and STIs are possible the first time — plan contraception before the wedding.

steps.title: Recovery takes time
steps.body: Many doctors suggest waiting until bleeding has stopped and the postnatal check (around 6 weeks), but readiness is personal — some take months. Stitches, caesarean wounds, tiredness and emotions all matter.

steps.title: Breastfeeding and dryness
steps.body: Breastfeeding lowers oestrogen, which can cause vaginal dryness. Lubricant helps. Breastfeeding also lowers desire for many people — this is normal.

steps.title: Fertility returns

steps.title: Pelvic floor
steps.body: Pelvic-floor exercises help bladder control and comfort. Persistent pain, leakage or low mood are reasons to see a doctor.

items.q: Is it normal not to want sex after a baby?
items.a: Very. Exhaustion, hormones and body changes are common reasons. Closeness can be rebuilt gradually.

items.q: Will it hurt?
items.a: It may feel different at first. Go slowly, use lubricant, and see a doctor if pain persists.

items.q: Can I get pregnant while breastfeeding?
items.a: Yes, unless strict conditions are met. Use contraception if you don't want another pregnancy soon.

lessons.title: Why do I suddenly smell? Sweat & body odour

scenes.text: Aarav, 14, lifts his arm after football and notices a sharp smell he never had at 11.
He worries everyone can smell him and stops raising his hand in class.
The school nurse explains it is puberty, not dirt — and gives him a two-minute routine.

steps.title: Two kinds of sweat glands
steps.body:
- **Eccrine glands** are all over the body and make watery, salty sweat that cools you. It has almost no smell.
- **Apocrine glands** sit in the armpits and groin and switch on at puberty. Their sweat is thicker, with fats and proteins.

Skin bacteria break down apocrine sweat into smelly compounds. That is why odour arrives with puberty.

steps.title: Sweat itself is nearly odourless
steps.body: Fresh sweat barely smells. The smell comes when bacteria have had a few hours to work on it — so washing and drying matter more than perfume.

steps.title: A routine that works
steps.body:
- Wash armpits, groin and feet daily with soap and water
- Dry fully (bacteria love damp)
- Use a deodorant (masks/fights bacteria) or antiperspirant (reduces sweat) on dry skin
- Change socks and innerwear daily; cotton breathes better
- Wash sports kit after every use

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Sweating that soaks clothes without heat or exercise (possible **hyperhidrosis**), night sweats with weight loss or fever, or a sudden new body smell (fruity breath, fishy or ammonia odour) are worth a doctor's visit.

items.q: Is it normal that one armpit smells more?
items.a: Yes. Gland numbers and bacteria differ side to side, and your dominant arm often sweats more.

items.q: Do I need antiperspirant or deodorant?
items.a: Deodorant tackles smell; antiperspirant reduces wetness using aluminium salts. Either is fine for most teens — pick by your problem.

items.q: Why do my feet stink worse than my armpits?
items.a: Feet have many sweat glands and sit in closed shoes, so bacteria thrive. Alternate shoes so they dry, wear clean socks, and dry between toes.

items.q: Can food change how I smell?
items.a: Strong foods like garlic, onion and some spices can come out in sweat and breath for a few hours. It is temporary.

options: Eccrine sweat being smelly by itself
quiz.why: Apocrine glands switch on at puberty; skin bacteria turn their sweat into smelly compounds.

quiz.why: Antiperspirants use aluminium salts to temporarily plug sweat ducts; deodorants mainly fight smell.

quiz.why: Damp shoes feed bacteria; dryness and clean socks cut odour.

steps.title: Everyone passes gas
steps.body: Healthy people pass gas many times a day — figures of around 10–20 times are commonly quoted. Gas comes from swallowed air and from gut bacteria fermenting food that the small intestine did not absorb.

steps.title: What makes it smellier
steps.body: Most gas is odourless (nitrogen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen, sometimes methane). Smell comes from tiny amounts of **sulphur compounds**, more common after eggs, cabbage, cauliflower, onions, and protein-heavy meals.

steps.title: Burps and gurgles
steps.body: Burps release swallowed air — from gulping, fizzy drinks, chewing gum, talking while eating. Stomach rumbles (**borborygmi**) are muscles moving food and gas; they are louder when the stomach is empty.

steps.title: Reducing gas politely
steps.body:
- Eat slowly, mouth closed
- Cut fizzy drinks and gum
- Increase high-fibre foods gradually, with water
- Walk after meals
- In company: excuse yourself to the washroom — no one needs to know why

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Gas with severe pain, blood in stool, weight loss, ongoing diarrhoea, or symptoms after dairy/wheat every time (possible intolerance) → see a doctor.

statements.s: Holding in gas for a long time is dangerous.
statements.why: It may cause bloating and discomfort, but it is not dangerous; the gas is reabsorbed or released later.

statements.s: Fizzy drinks increase burping.
statements.why: The carbon dioxide in them has to come out somewhere.

statements.s: Smelly gas means you are unhealthy.
statements.why: Smell mostly reflects food (sulphur compounds), not illness.

statements.s: A loud stomach on an empty stomach is normal.
statements.why: Gut muscles keep moving even when empty — with less food to muffle the sound.

statements.s: Suddenly adding lots of fibre can increase gas for a while.
statements.why: Gut bacteria ferment fibre; increase it slowly so the gut adapts.

steps.title: Bad breath (halitosis)
steps.body: Most bad breath starts in the mouth: bacteria on the back of the tongue, between teeth and in gum pockets. Morning breath is normal because saliva drops at night.

steps.title: What fixes it
steps.body:
- Brush twice daily for two minutes and **clean your tongue**
- Floss or use interdental brushes
- Drink water; dry mouth smells
- Treat gum bleeding — see a dentist
- Avoid tobacco and gutka (they cause odour and much worse)

steps.title: Sweaty palms and blushing
steps.body: Sweaty palms before exams are the stress (fight-or-flight) system. Blushing is extra blood flow to facial skin. Both are harmless; breathing slowly and accepting it reduces it.

steps.title: When breath signals illness
steps.body: Persistent bad breath despite good hygiene, a fruity smell (can occur with uncontrolled diabetes), or with sinus/throat pain — see a dentist or doctor.

items.q: How can I check my own breath?
items.a: Lick the inside of your wrist, let it dry for a few seconds, and smell. Or ask someone you trust — it is a kind question.

items.q: Is mouthwash enough?
items.a: It masks smell for an hour or so. Brushing, tongue cleaning and flossing remove the cause.

items.q: Why do I get white lumps in my tonsils that smell?
items.a: These are often tonsil stones — trapped debris. Gargling helps; if frequent or painful, see an ENT doctor.

items.q: My face goes red when I talk. Can I stop it?
items.a: Trying hard not to blush often makes it worse. Most people notice it far less than you think.

scenes.text: Ananya, 13, notices white-yellowish stains on her underwear and thinks something is wrong.
Her aunt, a nurse, explains discharge usually starts 6–12 months before the first period and is healthy.

steps.title: What discharge is
steps.body: Vaginal discharge is fluid from glands in the cervix and vagina. It keeps the vagina moist, carries away old cells, and its slightly acidic environment helps protect against infection. The vagina is self-cleaning.

steps.title: How it changes
steps.body:
- After a period: little, drier
- Around mid-cycle (ovulation): clear, stretchy, slippery, more of it
- Before a period: thicker, white or creamy
- Dried discharge on underwear may look yellowish — that is normal

steps.title: Signs worth checking
steps.body:
- Strong fishy smell, especially after washing
- Green or grey colour, frothy
- Thick, cottage-cheese-like with itching (often yeast)
- Itching, burning, pain, sores, or bleeding between periods

These are common and treatable — see a doctor rather than self-treating.

steps.title: Hygiene: less is more
steps.body: Wash the outer area (vulva) with plain water or mild unscented soap. **Do not douche** or use scented washes inside — they upset the natural balance and can cause infections. Cotton underwear, changed daily.

items.q: Is it normal to have discharge every day?
items.a: Yes. Amount varies person to person and through the month.

items.q: Can I use intimate washes or perfume?
items.a: Not needed and can irritate. Water or mild unscented soap outside only.

items.q: Does discharge mean I've had sex or caught something?
items.a: No. Discharge is normal for everyone with a vagina after puberty starts. Only changes in smell/colour/itch need checking.

items.q: Is a panty liner every day okay?
items.a: Occasionally fine; daily use can trap moisture. Choose breathable, unscented ones and change often.

quiz.q: Clear, stretchy discharge mid-cycle is usually…
quiz.why: Cervical mucus becomes clear and stretchy near ovulation.

options: White creamy discharge before a period
Green, frothy discharge with a strong smell
quiz.why: Colour/odour changes plus itching suggest infection.

options: Not recommended — it disturbs the natural balance
The best way to prevent infection
quiz.why: The vagina is self-cleaning; douching raises infection risk.
It is one of the signs a first period is approaching.

lessons.title: Period surprises: clots, smells, irregular cycles

scenes.text: Meera, 15, tracks her cycle: 24 days, then 38, then 31.
She fears something is broken.
Her doctor says cycles often take a few years to settle.

steps.title: What is 'normal'
steps.body: In adults, cycles of about 21–35 days are typical; bleeding usually lasts 2–7 days. In the first years after the first period, cycles of up to about 45 days and irregularity are common because ovulation isn't regular yet.

steps.title: Clots and colour
steps.body: Small clots (smaller than a ₹1 coin, roughly) on heavy days are common. Brown blood at the start or end is older blood. A mild metallic smell is normal.

steps.title: See a doctor if
steps.body:
- Soaking a pad/tampon every 1–2 hours for several hours
- Clots larger than about 2.5 cm, often
- Periods lasting more than 7 days
- No period by 15, or none for 3+ months after being regular
- Pain that stops school or isn't helped by usual pain relief
- Dizziness, breathlessness (possible anaemia)

steps.title: Why periods go missing
steps.body: Stress, sudden weight change, intense exercise, illness, thyroid issues, PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) — and, if sexually active, pregnancy. A doctor can check calmly.

statements.s: Cycles may be irregular for the first couple of years after the first period.
statements.why: Hormonal patterns take time to settle.

statements.s: You cannot get pregnant during your period.
statements.why: Unlikely but possible, especially with short cycles; sperm can survive several days.

statements.s: Severe pain that stops you going to school is just something to put up with.
statements.why: That can signal conditions like endometriosis — see a doctor.

statements.s: Brown blood at the end of a period is usually old blood.
statements.why: Blood that has taken longer to leave darkens.

lessons.title: Nightfall: what a wet dream is (and isn't)

scenes.text: Rohan, 14, wakes up with wet, sticky shorts.
He thinks he's ill or did something wrong.
His uncle tells him calmly it's a normal part of growing up.

steps.title: What happens
steps.body: During puberty the testes start making sperm and the body makes semen. During sleep, sometimes with a dream and sometimes without, the body releases semen. This is a **nocturnal emission** (wet dream, 'nightfall', 'swapnadosh').

steps.title: How common
steps.body: Most boys have them at some point during adolescence; some have them often, some rarely or never. All are normal. They usually become less frequent with age.

steps.title: Myth: 'losing strength' or 'one drop = 40 drops of blood'
steps.body: False. Semen is made continuously from body fluids; losing it does not cause weakness, poor eyesight, hair loss or infertility. Clinics selling 'nightfall cures' exploit fear — avoid them.

steps.title: Practical
steps.body: Rinse underwear or put it in the wash, shower, carry on. No need to tell anyone unless you want to. If you feel guilty, remember: it is involuntary.

items.q: Can I stop wet dreams?
items.a: Not really, and there's no need. They're involuntary. They often decrease with age.

items.q: Does it mean I'm thinking 'dirty' thoughts?
items.a: No. Dreams happen on their own; many wet dreams happen without any dream you remember.

items.q: Is it a disease called 'dhat'?
items.a: 'Dhat syndrome' describes anxiety about semen loss, a culture-linked worry — not a physical disease. If worry is strong, a doctor or counsellor can help.

items.q: Do girls have something similar?
items.a: People of any sex can have sexual dreams and arousal during sleep. It's normal too.

steps.title: Why they happen
steps.body: Erections can happen without any sexual thought — from hormones, a full bladder, friction, or randomly. In puberty they are frequent. During sleep, several erections per night are normal (linked to REM sleep), so waking with one is common.

steps.title: If it happens in public

steps.title: What research shows
steps.body: A large review of measurements (Veale et al., 2015, about 15,000 men) found an average erect length of about 13 cm and flaccid about 9 cm. Most people are close to average. Flaccid size varies with cold, stress and exercise. Growth continues until the late teens.

steps.title: Why online images mislead
steps.body: Pornography selects for unusual bodies, uses camera angles and editing. Comparing yourself to it is like comparing your face to a filtered film poster. 'Enlargement' pills, oils and devices sold online don't work and some are harmful.

steps.title: Breasts
steps.body: Breasts develop over several years. One being bigger than the other is very common. Boys can get temporary breast swelling (**gynaecomastia**) during puberty — usually settles in months to two years. Size has nothing to do with milk-making ability or health.

steps.title: Testicular self-check (from mid-teens)
steps.body: Once a month after a warm shower: gently roll each testicle between thumb and fingers. Normal: one may hang lower; the epididymis is a soft tube at the back. Report a new hard lump, swelling or heaviness to a doctor. Sudden severe testicle pain is an **emergency** (possible torsion) — go to hospital immediately.

items.q: Is one testicle lower normal?
items.a: Yes, very common.

items.q: Do breast-size creams work?
items.a: No reliable evidence. Breast size mainly depends on genes and body fat.

items.q: Is my penis curved — is that a problem?
items.a: Mild curves are common. Pain, a new bend or lumps should be checked.

items.q: I'm a boy with puffy nipples. Is that normal?
items.a: Puberty gynaecomastia is common and usually goes away. See a doctor if it's painful, one-sided and hard, or lasts beyond 2 years.

scenes.text: Zoya, 15, notices dark hair on her upper lip; a cousin teases her.
Her mother explains hair is normal; removal is optional.

steps.title: Why hair appears
steps.body: At puberty, androgens (hormones present in all sexes) make fine hair thicker and darker in armpits, pubic area, legs, and in many people the face and chest. Amount depends mostly on genes and ethnicity.

steps.title: Your body, your choice
steps.body: Removing hair is cultural and personal, not a hygiene need. Pubic hair actually protects skin from friction.

steps.title: When to check
steps.body: Sudden heavy hair growth in a female-bodied person, especially with irregular periods, acne or weight gain, can be linked to **PCOS** — worth a doctor's visit.

steps.title: Safe removal
steps.body:
- Shave with a clean sharp razor, wet skin, in the direction of hair growth; don't share razors
- Trim instead of shaving to avoid bumps
- Patch-test hair-removal creams; never on broken skin
- Waxing: hygienic salon, avoid on irritated skin

items.q: Does shaving make hair grow back thicker?
items.a: No. The cut tip feels blunt and stubbly, but thickness and colour don't change.

items.q: Is chest hair on girls or no beard on boys normal?
items.a: Both are normal variations.

items.q: What's an ingrown hair?
items.a: A hair that curls back into skin causing a red bump. Exfoliate gently, don't dig at it; see a doctor if it's painful or pus-filled.

items.q: Why is my underarm skin darker?
items.a: Friction, shaving and genetics often darken skin. A velvety thick dark patch on the neck or armpits (acanthosis nigricans) can be linked to insulin resistance — mention it to a doctor.

steps.title: How a spot forms
steps.body: Hormones increase skin oil (sebum). Oil plus dead skin cells blocks a pore (blackhead/whitehead). Bacteria and inflammation turn it into a red spot.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- Not caused by dirt (blackheads are oxidised oil)
- Chocolate isn't a proven cause; high-sugar diets and dairy may matter for some
- Toothpaste irritates skin
- Squeezing raises scarring risk

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Gentle cleanser twice a day
- Non-comedogenic moisturiser and sunscreen
- Over-the-counter options such as benzoyl peroxide or adapalene, used as the label says
- Patience: 8–12 weeks to see change
- See a dermatologist for painful, deep or scarring acne

steps.title: Mental health
steps.body: Acne can hurt confidence. If it's affecting your mood, that's a valid reason to see a doctor.

statements.s: Acne is caused by not washing.

steps.title: Stretch marks
steps.body: They happen when skin stretches quickly (growth spurts, weight change, pregnancy, muscle gain). Red/purple at first, they fade to silvery lines. Creams make little difference; they are harmless.

steps.title: Moles: the ABCDE check
steps.body: See a doctor if a mole shows **A**symmetry, irregular **B**order, several **C**olours, **D**iameter over ~6 mm, or is **E**volving (changing, bleeding, itching).

steps.title: Other common things
steps.body: Keratosis pilaris (rough bumps on upper arms), white patches after fungal infection, and dandruff are common and treatable.

items.q: Can I get rid of stretch marks?
items.a: They fade naturally. Treatments by dermatologists can improve appearance but rarely remove them.

items.q: Are white patches always vitiligo?
items.a: No — many are fungal or post-inflammatory. A doctor can tell the difference.

items.q: Is vitiligo contagious?
items.a: No. It's an autoimmune condition; it's not infectious and not caused by food combinations.

items.q: Are fairness creams safe?
items.a: Some contain hidden steroids or mercury that damage skin. Avoid unknown 'fairness' products; all skin tones are healthy.

scenes.text: Vikram, 29, a coder, sees bright red blood on toilet paper and is too embarrassed to tell anyone.
His GP diagnoses piles; fibre, water and movement help within weeks.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: What piles are
steps.body: Haemorrhoids are swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal. Everyone has these cushions; they become 'piles' when they swell or slip. Internal piles often bleed painlessly (bright red); external ones can be itchy, lumpy or painful if a clot forms.

steps.title: Fissure
steps.body: A small tear in the anal lining, usually from passing hard stool: sharp pain during and after a motion, sometimes with blood. Often heals with softer stools.

steps.title: First-line care
steps.body:
- Fibre: whole grains, dal, fruit, vegetables; fluids
- Don't strain or sit on the toilet scrolling
- Respond to the urge; don't delay
- Warm sitz baths
- Pharmacist creams for symptom relief
- Move: long sitting worsens it

steps.title: Red flags — see a doctor
steps.body: Rectal bleeding at any age the first time; especially over 40, with change in bowel habit lasting weeks, dark/maroon blood, weight loss, anaemia, or family history of bowel cancer. Never assume all bleeding is piles.

activity.prompt: Questions people whisper at the pharmacy

items.q: Is surgery always needed?
items.a: No. Most piles settle with diet and habits; procedures like banding are for persistent cases.

items.q: Does spicy food cause piles?
items.a: It doesn't cause them, but can irritate. Constipation and straining are bigger factors.

items.q: Are piles common in pregnancy?
items.a: Yes — pressure and hormones; treatment is mostly the same gentle measures.

items.q: Is scrolling on the toilet really a problem?
items.a: Long sitting increases pressure on the cushions. Keep toilet time short.

quiz.why: Typical, but doctors must exclude other causes.

steps.title: What a UTI is
steps.body: Bacteria (most often E. coli from the gut) enter the urethra and infect the bladder (cystitis). Women get them more often because the urethra is shorter and closer to the anus. Men, children and older adults get them too.

steps.title: Symptoms
steps.body: Burning/stinging when peeing, frequency, urgency, cloudy or smelly urine, lower tummy pain, sometimes blood.

steps.title: Upper-tract warning signs
steps.body: Fever, chills, back/side pain, vomiting → possible kidney infection — seek care the same day. In pregnancy, men, children, or with blood in urine, always see a doctor.

steps.title: Why not leftover antibiotics
steps.body: Wrong drug, wrong dose, or too short a course fails to clear infection and drives **antimicrobial resistance**. India has high resistance rates for common UTI bugs; doctors may need a urine culture.

steps.title: Prevention (helpful habits)
steps.body: Drink enough water, don't hold urine long, wipe front to back, pee after sex, avoid scented products around the genitals.

statements.s: UTIs are more common in women because of a shorter urethra.
Fever with back pain and a UTI can mean kidney infection.

statements.s: Men can't get UTIs.
statements.why: Less common, but they do — and need a check.

steps.body: Doctors call it the 'door-handle moment' — people mention the main worry as they leave. Say it first: 'The thing I'm most worried about is…'

steps.title: SOCRATES-lite

items.q: Do I need to tell the doctor I drink, smoke or use drugs?

items.q: Will they judge my weight / my sex life?

items.q: I googled my symptoms — should I say?

steps.title: Consent
steps.body: Before an examination or procedure, you should be told what it is, why, and alternatives. You can ask questions, ask for a chaperone, and **withdraw consent at any time**.

steps.title: Intimate examinations

steps.title: Constitution, Article 22
steps.body: An arrested person must be informed of the grounds of arrest as soon as possible, has the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time).

steps.title: BNSS 2023

steps.title: Adult choice
steps.body: The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that adults' right to choose a partner is part of Article 21 (e.g. Shafin Jahan 2018, Shakti Vahini 2018 on 'honour' crimes).

steps.title: Special Marriage Act 1954
steps.body: Allows marriage between people of any religion without conversion; requires a 30-day notice period at the marriage officer's office; minimum ages 21 (man) and 18 (woman).

steps.title: Live-in
steps.body: Courts have held that live-in relationships between consenting adults are not illegal; women in a 'relationship in the nature of marriage' can seek protection under the Domestic Violence Act 2005. Uttarakhand's Uniform Civil Code (2024) requires registration of live-in relationships there.

steps.title: PWDVA 2005
steps.body: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act covers physical, sexual, verbal/emotional and economic abuse; remedies include protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief and custody. Protection Officers and service providers help file complaints.

steps.title: Criminal law
steps.body: Cruelty by husband or relatives is an offence under the BNS (earlier IPC 498A); dowry death provisions also exist.

steps.title: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005
steps.body: Daughters are coparceners by birth in Hindu joint family property, with the same rights and liabilities as sons. In Vineeta Sharma (2020) the Supreme Court held this applies regardless of whether the father was alive on the 2005 amendment date.

steps.title: Other laws
steps.body: Muslims, Christians, Parsis and others have their own succession laws (e.g. Muslim personal law; Indian Succession Act 1925).

scenes.text: Nisha, 17, standing near the edge, gets a flash: 'What if I jumped?'

steps.title: What they are
steps.body: Intrusive thoughts are unwanted, sudden thoughts, images or urges that feel out of character — violent, sexual, blasphemous, embarrassing. Research across countries has found the large majority of people report having them.

steps.title: Why the brain does it
steps.body: The brain constantly generates 'what if' predictions, including about dangers. A thought popping up is noise; the distress comes from interpreting it as meaningful ('I must be a bad person').

steps.title: Thought ≠ intention
steps.body: Intrusive thoughts feel **ego-dystonic** — alien, repugnant to you. That horror is itself evidence they don't reflect your wishes.

steps.title: Different from suicidal thinking
steps.body: If thoughts about ending your life feel wanted, comforting, or you're making plans, that's different — please talk to someone today: Tele-MANAS 14416, or 112 in an emergency.

items.q: I imagined hurting my baby/sibling. Am I dangerous?
items.a: Such thoughts are common, especially in new parents. Being horrified by them is typical of intrusive thoughts, not intent. If they're frequent and distressing, a doctor can help — this is treatable.

items.q: I had a blasphemous thought in a temple/church/mosque. Am I sinning?
items.a: Many faith traditions and clinicians recognise unwanted thoughts as not chosen. Religious scrupulosity is a known OCD theme and responds to treatment.

items.q: Why do they get worse when I try to stop them?
items.a: Trying hard to suppress a thought makes the brain check for it — the rebound effect.

items.q: Should I tell anyone?
items.a: Saying it to a trusted person or therapist often shrinks the fear dramatically.

steps.title: OCD in brief
steps.body: Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves **obsessions** (intrusive thoughts causing distress) plus **compulsions** (repeated actions or mental rituals to neutralise them) that take a lot of time (often > 1 hour/day) or impair life.

steps.title: Treatment works

steps.title: Sleep stages
steps.body: Sleep cycles roughly every 90 minutes through light sleep, deep sleep and **REM** (rapid eye movement) sleep. Vivid, story-like dreams happen most in REM, which grows longer towards morning.

steps.title: Why strange
steps.body: In REM, emotional and visual brain areas are active while areas for logic and time-checking are quieter — so impossible plots feel real.

steps.title: Common themes
steps.body: Being chased, falling, teeth falling out, exams, being late, being unprepared — reported across cultures. Often linked to stress, not prophecy.

steps.title: No proof of prediction
steps.body: There's no scientific evidence dreams predict the future. Treat dream 'meanings' as reflection, not fact.

items.q: Why do I dream of people who died?
items.a: Grief often appears in dreams; many find it comforting or upsetting. Both are normal.

items.q: I had a sexual dream about someone unexpected. Does it mean something?
items.a: Dreams remix people and feelings randomly. It doesn't define your desires.

items.q: Why can't I remember dreams?
items.a: You remember mainly when you wake during or right after REM.

items.q: Do nightmares mean I'm ill?
items.a: Occasional nightmares are normal. Frequent ones after trauma deserve professional help.

lessons.title: Sleep paralysis: the 'ghost on the chest'

steps.title: What happens
steps.body: In REM sleep your muscles are temporarily paralysed (**atonia**) so you don't act out dreams. Sometimes you wake before atonia ends: you're conscious but can't move for seconds to a couple of minutes.

steps.title: Why the 'presence'
steps.body: Dream imagery can leak into waking — figures, pressure on the chest, sounds. Cultures name it differently (spirits, 'jinn', 'old hag'). It's harmless.

steps.title: Reduce it
steps.body: Regular sleep times, enough sleep, less sleeping on your back for some people, limit alcohol. During an episode: focus on moving a toe or finger; breathe slowly; remind yourself it'll pass.

steps.title: Hypnic jerks
steps.body: The sudden 'falling' jolt as you drift off is a hypnic jerk — common, harmless, more likely when tired, stressed or after caffeine.

statements.why: It's REM atonia persisting into waking.

steps.title: Fight-or-flight
steps.body: Adrenaline raises heart rate, speeds breathing, tenses muscles and redirects blood. Fast breathing lowers carbon dioxide, causing tingling, dizziness and chest tightness — which feel like danger, so the alarm grows.

steps.title: Timeline
steps.body: Panic attacks build quickly, typically peaking within about 10 minutes, and then subside. They're very unpleasant but not dangerous in themselves.

steps.title: Don't self-diagnose chest pain
steps.body: If it's your first episode, or chest pain is crushing, spreads to arm/jaw, comes with exertion, or you have heart risk factors — call 112. Ruling out a heart problem is always okay.

steps.title: Common symptoms
steps.body: Pounding heart, sweating, shaking, breathlessness, choking feeling, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, tingling, feeling unreal, fear of losing control or dying.

lessons.title: The last days: what families often see

scenes.text: Dadi, 88, sleeps most of the day and stops eating.
A palliative nurse explains these are natural changes and how to keep her comfortable.

steps.title: Common changes
steps.body: Near the end, people often sleep more, eat and drink little, become confused at times, have cool hands and feet, and breathing patterns change — periods of fast breathing and pauses. A rattling sound can come from secretions in the throat; it's usually not distressing to the person.

steps.title: Hearing
steps.body: Hearing is thought to be one of the last senses to fade, so families are encouraged to keep talking softly.

steps.title: Palliative care
steps.body: Palliative care focuses on comfort — pain, breathlessness, anxiety — for any serious illness, not only the last days. Hospitals and organisations in India increasingly offer it, including at home.

steps.title: Comfort
steps.body: Moisten lips, reposition gently, keep the room calm, play favourite music or prayers, hold hands.

items.q: Should we force food or water?
items.a: Loss of appetite is natural near death; forcing can cause discomfort. Ask the care team about mouth care.

items.q: Is the rattling breath painful?
items.a: Usually not for the person; nurses can reposition or give medicine to ease it.

items.q: Should children be present?
items.a: If they want and are prepared for what they'll see, many find it meaningful. Never force.

items.q: What if they die when I step out?
items.a: This happens often. It's not your failure.

steps.title: Immediately
steps.body: If death is expected at home, call the family doctor/palliative team to confirm and issue a medical cause-of-death certificate. If unexpected, call 112. In hospitals, staff confirm and guide you.

steps.title: Registration
steps.body: Under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, deaths should be reported/registered with the local registrar (municipality/panchayat) — within **21 days** is the standard window. The death certificate is needed for bank, insurance, property and pension.

steps.title: Police involvement
steps.body: Accidents, suspected unnatural deaths or deaths in custody involve police and possibly a post-mortem. This is routine law, not an accusation.

steps.title: Practical list
steps.body: Inform close family, decide rites per faith/wishes, keep the medical certificate, get several copies of the death certificate, notify bank/employer/insurer, look for a will and nominations.

steps.body: Brain-stem death is legally recognised in India under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994. It's confirmed by a board of doctors through formal tests; it's not a coma.

steps.title: Donation
steps.body: One deceased donor can help several people (kidneys, liver, heart, lungs, corneas and tissues). Families consent; pledging your wish and telling family helps. Eyes can be donated after ordinary death within hours.

steps.title: Whole-body donation

steps.title: Misconception
steps.body: Donation doesn't prevent open-casket viewing or religious rites in general; most major faiths support it.

steps.title: Beyond 'five stages'
steps.body: The well-known 'five stages' (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) came from work with dying patients and are not a fixed sequence. Many researchers describe grief as oscillating between loss-focused and life-focused moments (the 'dual process' model).

steps.title: Common experiences
steps.body: Waves of sadness, anger, guilt, relief (after long illness), numbness, poor sleep, appetite changes, forgetfulness, sensing the person's presence, dreams of them.

steps.title: Prolonged grief
steps.body: When intense yearning and inability to function persist for a long time (around 12 months or more in adults, per DSM-5-TR), it may be prolonged grief disorder — treatable with specialised therapy.

steps.title: Self-care
steps.body: Routine, food, sleep, sharing memories, rituals, and permission to have good moments.

steps.body: 'I'm not able to lend money right now, but I can help you look at other options.' No long justification needed.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Absorption & effects
steps.body: Ethanol is absorbed from the stomach and small intestine into the blood within minutes; food slows it. It's a central nervous system **depressant**: first lowering inhibition, then slowing judgment, coordination, reaction time, and at high levels breathing.

steps.title: Metabolism
steps.body: The liver breaks down alcohol at a roughly fixed rate — very roughly one standard drink per hour. Coffee, cold showers or vomiting don't speed it up.

steps.title: WHO position
steps.body: WHO (2023) states there is no level of alcohol consumption that is safe for health; alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen linked to several cancers.

steps.title: Blackouts
steps.body: High blood alcohol blocks the hippocampus from forming new memories — a blackout, a sign of dangerous drinking.

items.q: Does beer get you less drunk than whisky?
items.a: No. It's the amount of alcohol that matters — a beer, a glass of wine and a peg of spirits can each be about one standard drink.

items.q: Does eating before drinking prevent getting drunk?
items.a: It slows absorption but doesn't prevent intoxication.

items.q: Why do some people's faces go red?
items.a: Often an inherited enzyme variant (ALDH2) causing acetaldehyde build-up — common in East Asian ancestry; linked to higher oesophageal cancer risk if they drink.

items.q: Can I sober up fast?
items.a: No. Only time lowers blood alcohol.

options: Failure to form memories due to high alcohol

steps.title: Signs of alcohol poisoning
steps.body: Confusion, vomiting, seizures, slow or irregular breathing (<8 breaths/min or gaps >10 s), blue/pale skin, low temperature, can't be woken.

steps.title: What to do
steps.body:
- Call **112**
- Don't leave them alone
- If breathing but unresponsive, place in the **recovery position** (on their side) to prevent choking on vomit
- Keep warm
- Don't give coffee, cold showers, or more alcohol; don't make them walk or vomit
- Tell paramedics what and how much they drank

steps.title: Why 'sleep it off' kills
steps.body: Blood alcohol can keep rising after the last drink as alcohol is absorbed; breathing and gag reflexes can fail during sleep.

steps.title: Note

steps.title: THC and CBD
steps.body: Cannabis contains cannabinoids. **THC** is the main intoxicating one; it binds CB1 receptors in the brain's endocannabinoid system, affecting memory, coordination, appetite, time perception and mood. **CBD** isn't intoxicating in the same way.

steps.title: Potency has risen
steps.body: Many modern products contain far more THC than decades ago, raising risks.

steps.title: Short-term effects
steps.body: Relaxation or euphoria, altered perception, slowed reaction time, impaired short-term memory, red eyes, increased appetite — and for some, anxiety, panic, or paranoia.

steps.title: 'Natural' ≠ safe
steps.body: Many natural substances are harmful (tobacco, arsenic). Risk depends on dose, potency, age and frequency.

Natural means harmless.
Cannabis can cause anxiety or paranoia in some people.

steps.title: Developing brain
steps.body: The brain develops into the mid-20s. Regular use starting in adolescence is associated with problems in attention, memory and learning, and greater risk of dependence.

steps.title: Psychosis
steps.body: Frequent use of high-potency cannabis is associated with increased risk of psychotic disorders, particularly in young people and those with family history.

steps.title: Cannabis use disorder
steps.body: Some users develop dependence: cravings, needing more, failing to cut down, withdrawal (irritability, poor sleep, low appetite).

steps.title: If you choose to cut down
steps.body: Set use-free days, avoid triggers, tell a friend, seek help from a doctor/de-addiction service (Tele-MANAS 14416).

items.q: Can you get addicted to weed?
items.a: Yes, some people do — risk is higher with early, daily, high-potency use.

items.q: Is it less harmful than alcohol?
items.a: They have different harms; neither is risk-free. Mixing them increases impairment.

items.q: Does it cure anxiety?
items.a: It may feel calming briefly, but it can worsen anxiety and panic, particularly high-THC products.

items.q: What's a 'greening out'?
items.a: Feeling very unwell (nausea, dizziness, panic) after too much. Sit down, sip water, stay with someone; call 112 if severe.

lessons.title: The NDPS Act: what's legal and what isn't

scenes.text: At Holi, bhang thandai is served openly. 'So weed is legal?' asks Priya.

steps.title: NDPS Act 1985
steps.body: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act defines **cannabis** to include ganja (flowering tops) and charas (resin), and their mixtures. Cultivation, production, possession, sale, purchase, transport and use are offences, with punishment scaling with quantity (small, intermediate, commercial).

steps.title: Bhang
steps.body: Cannabis leaves and seeds (used for bhang) are excluded from the NDPS definition of ganja; bhang is regulated by state excise laws, with licensed sale in some states and bans in others.

steps.title: Small quantity
steps.body: Even small-quantity ganja possession is punishable (rigorous imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both). Section 64A provides possible immunity from prosecution for addicts charged with small-quantity consumption offences who volunteer for de-addiction treatment.

steps.title: Travelling abroad
steps.body: Countries' laws differ hugely; some impose severe penalties. Never carry anything for someone else.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: How much
steps.body: Many food-safety bodies advise healthy adults keep caffeine to about 400 mg/day; less for adolescents and in pregnancy. A cup of brewed coffee often has ~80–120 mg; energy drink cans vary widely — check the label.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body: Caffeine blocks adenosine (the 'sleepy' signal): alertness, but also jitters, fast heartbeat, anxiety, stomach upset, poor sleep. Mixing with alcohol masks drunkenness, leading to more drinking.

steps.title: Better exam fuel
steps.body: Sleep, water, regular meals, short walks. Avoid caffeine late in the day.

bands.text: Around the common adult upper guidance; teens should be lower.
Above typical guidance — jitters, palpitations, anxiety, sleep loss likely. Very high doses can be dangerous.

scenes.text: A senior offers 'focus pills' (prescription stimulants) and 'sleep tablets' bought without prescription.

steps.title: Stimulants
steps.body: Prescription stimulants for ADHD are safe-ish under medical supervision. Without one, they can cause palpitations, anxiety, insomnia, high blood pressure, and dependence; evidence they improve exam performance in people without ADHD is weak.

steps.title: Sedatives
steps.body: Benzodiazepines and similar sleeping pills cause dependence with regular use, impair memory and coordination, and are dangerous with alcohol or opioids.

steps.title: Codeine syrups
steps.body: Codeine-containing cough syrups are misused in parts of India; codeine is an opioid with addiction and overdose risk.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: Many such drugs are Schedule H/H1 (prescription-only) and some are controlled under the NDPS Act; selling or sharing them without prescription is illegal.
